acute

/uh-KYOOT/ — rhymes with 'a flute' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Acute is felt or experienced to an intense, sharp degree.

He felt acute embarrassment when his phone rang loudly during the silent exam.

Example

Halfway up the trail, Priya's ankle twisted on a loose rock. The pain was so acute — sharp and overwhelming — that she couldn't take another step, and her friends had to help her back down the mountain.

Acute means felt at an intense, piercing degree. 'Mild' discomfort lets you keep hiking; acute pain stops you cold.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

intense: Intense means existing in a very strong degree — heat, effort, or feeling can all be intense. It measures strength alone and says nothing about sharpness or suddenness. Acute adds the cutting edge: acute pain is piercing rather than merely strong, and in medicine acute strikes suddenly instead of lasting for years.

severe: Severe means very serious or harsh — a severe storm, a severe shortage. It measures how bad something is, not how suddenly it arrives or how sharply it is felt. Acute carries both of those extra ideas: a sharp, piercing quality, and in medicine a sudden onset.

piercing: Piercing means sharp enough to cut through — a piercing whistle, a piercing wind. It names the sharp quality of the thing itself, while acute describes how intensely a person feels or experiences something. A siren is piercing; the distress it stirs in a listener is acute.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

mild: gentle and not strong

dull: weak, blunted, not sharp

Where it sits · how overwhelming the sensation is — noticeable → acute → excruciating

noticeable vs. acute: Noticeable is weaker than acute — a noticeable feeling registers, but an acute one dominates everything else you sense.

excruciating vs. acute: Excruciating is stronger than acute — acute pain is intense, but excruciating pain is unbearable torture.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — acu-

root — acu-: needle, sharp point (Latin)

suffix — -te (-tus)

suffix — -te (-tus): having been made so (participle ending) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin acuere meant 'to sharpen.' Something acute has been 'sharpened to a point' — pain, senses, or a crisis felt at needle-sharp intensity.
